items.title: Algorithmic HRM and freelancer capabilities in Sri Lanka: constraints and the role of social support
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how algorithmic human resource management (HRM) constrains the capabilities of platform-based freelancers in Sri Lanka, and how informal social support helps them sustain these capabilities. Design/methodology/approach Using a qualitative design, the research draws on 41 in-depth interviews and applies reflexive thematic analysis, informed by the capability approach and social support theory. Findings Four interconnected themes were identified: algorithmic work allocation constrains income security and temporal autonomy, digital enforcement and dispute processes undermine procedural fairness and recognition, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven market changes constrain capabilities through skill devaluation, and informal social support functions as an extra-platform capability infrastructure. Practical implications The findings point to implications for platform design, regulatory policy and emerging forms of worker organising, particularly in contexts marked by weak institutional protections. Originality/value This study draws on the capability approach and social support theory to make two contributions. First, it identifies a cumulative, reputation-based pathway through which algorithmic HRM constrains capabilities in knowledge-intensive freelancing. This extends current understanding beyond the transaction-based gig work that has dominated prior research. Second, it shows that informal social support contributes directly to capability development but cannot alter the structural algorithmic mechanisms that govern visibility, income security and procedural voice.

items.title: Algorithmic management and occupational health and safety: Non-deterministic insights into a contested relation
items.abstract: This article examines the relationship between algorithmic management and occupational health and safety (OHS) through the lens of Labour Process Theory, situating technology within the contested terrain of workplace control. Debates often isolate algorithmic management from the structural dynamics of managerial prerogative, overlooking how they relate to OHS risks. Using data from an European representative survey, this exploratory study assesses how automated work attribution and biological indicators monitoring condition workplace risks. Findings show divergent moderating patterns: these tools are associated with lower probabilities of detrimental OHS outcomes in some configurations, but higher probabilities in others. The moderating role of these tools varies considerably across different work environment configurations, and the magnitude of the associated shifts in probability is never enough to equalise scenarios where “traditional” risks are absent. Ultimately, the integration of technology can only be successful when done critically and without losing sight of broader workplace sources of risk.

items.title: Alternative creativity: why generative AI is creative, and why it is not like us
items.abstract: Abstract Whether generative artificial intelligence is creative is usually argued as a yes-or-no question, and both camps share an unexamined assumption, that there is one kind of creativity, the human kind, which the machine either has or lacks. This article defends a third position, alternative creativity. For any fixed medium the set of possible artefacts is finite and astronomically large, and almost none of it is valuable. Creativity, wherever it occurs, is therefore a compression of that space into a small manifold of meaningful candidates, followed by a value-guided search across the manifold. On the leading neuroscientific account, human brains work this way, and generative models demonstrably do. Neither creates from nothing, both recombine what they have internalised, both use constrained randomness, and both hold their skills in the strengths of their connections. In these respects the two are less different than is commonly supposed. Where they differ is in how the connections were shaped and in what each creator can reach at the moment of creation. A person's parameters are formed by a body acting in a physical and social world, a model's by an archive of what people have said and shown, and this difference in accessible context, together with a difference in how value is grounded, explains more of the divergence in what the two creators make than the difference of substrate does. In domains with checkable answers, machines already search beyond the human distribution under verifiable rewards. In the arts, where no verifier exists, they must borrow taste from people. From this account the article derives the homogenisation of machine output, the general intractability of tracing outputs to training inputs, the migration of authorship towards the specification of value, and the logic of human–machine collaboration, in which each creator supplies what the other constitutionally cannot.

items.title: An agentic AI system enhances clinical detection of immune-related adverse events in a multi-phase validation study
items.abstract: Abstract Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affect up to 40% of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet identification requires laborious, inconsistent manual chart review. Here we show that agentic artificial intelligence coupled with human verification could enhance efficiency, performance and consistency for irAE assessment. We developed and evaluated an agentic large language model system to extract the presence, temporality, severity grade, attribution and certainty of six irAE types from clinical notes. Retrospectively, the system achieved a macro-averaged F 1 of 0.92 for current-event detection and 0.66 for multi-class severity grading; self-consistency improved F 1 by 0.14. The best-performing configuration cost approximately US$0.02 per note. In prospective silent deployment over 3 months, the binary F 1 was 0.72–0.79. In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff, agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 2.71 min ( P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (odds ratio 1.45; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.08; P = 0.045) and improved interannotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).

items.title: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Correlational Study of Students' Perceptions Following an AI-Supported Gamified Formative-Assessment Intervention
items.abstract: Abstract Against the growing integration of artificial intelligence in higher education, this study examines the mechanism through which AI-supported gamification is associated with language learning outcomes in university language courses in the Greater Bay Area. Drawing on self-determination theory and a formative assessment perspective, it develops and tests a conceptual model linking gamification attitudes, learning motivation, perceived AI use, and perceived language learning improvement. A quantitative survey yielded 72 valid responses. The measurement scale showed good internal consistency . In addition, a post-hoc power analysis using G*Power 3.1 indicated that, with , , and a moderate effect size , statistical power reached .90, suggesting that the sample size was adequate for regression-based analysis. The results showed that gamification attitudes were significantly and positively associated with perceived language learning improvement, while learning motivation was moderately and positively associated with improvement. Mediation analysis indicated that learning motivation significantly predicted perceived language learning improvement . After learning motivation was included in the model, the direct effect of gamification attitudes was no longer significant, and bootstrap analysis supported a full mediation pattern. Although perceived AI use did not show a significant direct effect on perceived language learning improvement, AI remained an important supportive element in the intervention. In this study, AI was embedded in a recurring feedback-revision-practice-diagnosis-reinforcement cycle, providing individualized formative feedback and informing subsequent gamified practice and teacher guidance. Overall, the findings suggest that AI-supported gamification may contribute to language learning outcomes primarily through its relationship with students’ learning motivation. The study offers practical implications for the design of motivation-oriented, AI-supported formative assessment in higher education language learning contexts.

items.title: Applications, ethics, and future agenda of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in tourism and hospitality: a systematic review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how tourism information is produced, exchanged, and consumed, yet its application scenarios, ethical consequences, and implications for service authenticity remain dispersed across a fast-growing literature. Following the PRISMA 2020 protocol, this study identifies 3,825 records from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus and conducts a thematic synthesis of 461 publications, addressing three questions: where GenAI creates value on the supply and demand sides of tourism and hospitality, which ethical risks and organizational dilemmas accompany its adoption, and how machine intervention conflicts with interactional authenticity in service encounters. The synthesis indicates that GenAI operates as a double-edged sword. On the demand side, conversational and multimodal systems lower information search and decision-making costs; on the supply side, automated content generation unlocks operational capacity—yet these gains coexist with algorithmic bias and hallucination, privacy trade-offs, and employee deskilling. In service interactions, the computational essence of machine-generated empathy can elicit expectancy violations and algorithm aversion, weakening the interpersonal authenticity on which hospitality depends. The review integrates these findings into an efficacy-risk hedging framework embedded in a socio-technical account of human-AI collaboration and derives a tiered human-in-the-loop governance model. Its primary contribution is to link application-level benefits, systemic risks, and the authenticity conflict within one evidence-based framework, with each claim anchored in article-level evidence counts.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) proposals to counter AI cheating by students in non-invigilated assessment
items.abstract: Since ChatGPT3′s chatbot interface appeared in November 2022, AI cheating has re-incarnated a challenge for academia. It is accentuated in non-invigilated contexts during term as projects, essays and other documents are submitted (possibly) prior to proctored examinations. Cheating can be interpreted strategically as the institutional level, whereas its tactical expression examined in this article applies at the student-instructor interface. Here, we turn AI upon itself to see if it can address the dilemma it has created. A literature review regarding AI-facilitated cheating precedes a record of public and initial academic reactions. Having calibrated the problem, a method for addressing it is advanced. It enlists a set of AI large language models (LLMs) and search engines to rank six techniques by effectiveness in countering AI cheating. Analysis includes: descriptive assessment of model outputs; frequency counting, ranking and determination of unique and common techniques; and qualitative comparison of the suggestions tendered. The discussion relates the characteristics of the composite approaches to traditional assessment and evaluation. Ideas for ongoing research, and key recommendations form the conclusions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Government Financial Reporting Transparency: Evidence from Nigeria's Federal Public Sector
items.abstract: Transparency is widely expected to sustain public trust in government, and artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a means of making public financial information more open, timely and understandable. This study examines whether the overall level of documented AI adoption is associated with the transparency of government financial reporting in Nigeria's federal public sector, and what the evidence implies for public trust. A balanced panel of five federal institutions: the Federal Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, the Federal Inland Revenue Service, the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Bureau of Public Procurement were observed from 2015 to 2024. Documentary evidence from annual reports, audit-related documents and AI-implementation documents is scored on a five-point (0–4) rubric and analysed with pooled, fixed-effects, trend-adjusted, first-difference and lagged regressions, interpreted through agency theory. Overall AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with transparency and credibility of financial reports (pooled β = 0.701, R² = 0.810; fixed-effects β = 0.708). Unlike the study's other AI–outcome relationships, however, this one is not robust throughout: the trend-adjusted coefficient (0.616) is only marginally significant (p = 0.051), and the first-difference coefficient (0.604) is not statistically significant (p = 0.112), although the lagged estimate (0.599) is. Transparency also has the lowest mean score of the five outcomes. The outcome is a documentary score of openness and credibility, not a survey of citizens, so the results speak to the supply of transparency and cannot establish public trust itself. Because the design is observational, the measures are documentary indices, and the sample is small and purposively selected, the results indicate association rather than proven causation and are interpreted for the five institutions examined rather than for all federal ministries, departments and agencies. AI adoption appears to be a helpful but insufficient condition for transparent reporting; communication, civic capacity and audit validation matter too.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Opportunities, Challenges, and Implications for the Learning Process
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping education faster than pedagogical theory and institutional policy can absorb it. Although reviews of AI in education (AIEd) are multiplying, most catalogue applications or list risks separately, leaving unclear how opportunities and challenges jointly reconfigure the learning process. This study addresses that gap through a systematic literature review guided by the PRISMA 2020 statement. Records were identified through the Consensus academic search engine using two search strings and supplemented by citation searching, then screened against criteria covering publication between 2021 and 2026, peer-reviewed status, an active DOI, and direct relevance to teaching and learning. Twenty-four studies were retained and analysed through thematic synthesis. The results reveal four clusters of opportunity: personalised and adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring and feedback, AI-supported assessment, and augmentation of teachers' work. These are counterbalanced by five clusters of challenge: academic integrity, algorithmic bias and data privacy, overreliance and the erosion of higher-order thinking, unequal infrastructure and AI literacy, and weak institutional governance. Mapping both clusters onto the stages of the learning process, the study proposes a Learner–Teacher–AI Agency Framework, which holds that AI improves learning only when it redistributes, rather than replaces, human agency. Implications are drawn for pedagogy, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and policy, particularly in developing-country contexts such as Indonesia.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education and graduate employability: cognitive engagement, self-efficacy, and career adaptability in the AI era
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used in higher education, but its contribution to graduate employability cannot be inferred from access to AI or frequency of use alone. This critical narrative review examines how AI-supported learning may relate to employability through processes discussed in educational psychology and career development. Searches of Web of Science, Scopus, ERIC, and PubMed covered database inception to 1 July 2026, with supplementary searches completed on 2 October 2026. The literature was synthesized interpretively and critically, with attention to the type of outcome measured and the extent to which findings support the proposed relationships. The synthesis focuses on cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, self-efficacy and motivational regulation, and career adaptability. Three tensions organize the discussion: capability augmentation and cognitive offloading, career agency and AI-related insecurity, and resource access and capability differences. Included studies report associations or short-term changes in outcomes such as engagement, AI literacy, self-efficacy, career adaptability, and perceived employability. Direct evidence linking AI-supported learning to later employment outcomes remains limited. The proposed framework should therefore be read as a set of theory-informed pathways for future testing, rather than as an established causal or temporal sequence. Implications for assessment, disciplinary AI literacy, career education, institutional support, and future research are discussed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Innovations in Obstetric and Primary Care: Clinical Applications and Future Prospects
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Background: AI is already integrated throughout the obstetric and primary care spectrum, ranging from automated ultrasound diagnosis interpretations, foetal monitoring, risk stratification for obstetric complications, to diagnostic decision support in primary care. Objectives: The aim of this review is to identify, summarize and highlight the literature on innovations in obstetric and primary care using artificial intelligence from 2020 to 2025, and to explore clinical applications, reported performance and challenges for use in daily practice. Method: Structured search of Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed-indexed sources was conducted using combinations of the terms “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “obstetrics,” “primary care,” “clinical decision support,” and specific applications (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and ultrasound) between 2020 and 2025. Findings: AI systems now have the ability of detecting foetal abnormalities and foetal biometry in the hospital setting and are approaching the accuracy of experts in obstetrics, with deep-learning models achieving even higher precision for foetal biometry and anomaly detection on ultrasound when compared with conventional risk-scoring methods. In the obstetrics setting, machine-learning models incorporating maternal traits, biophysical markers, and laboratory values predict preeclampsia and gestational diabetes, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve generally between 0.75 and 0.90, consistently outperforming traditional risk-scoring methods. AI-powered clinical decision support tools are being used in primary care to assist with diagnosis, risk stratification and documentation, but widespread adoption of these systems in the real world is more likely to be used for ambient scribing, decision support and workflow automation. In both areas, evidence quality is inconsistent, external evidence is scarce, and integration in clinical practice is inadequate compared to the development of the algorithm. Conclusion: AI is moving beyond the realm of research focus to become a new and growing clinical tool in obstetric and primary care; to achieve the potential of better outcomes for maternal, foetal, and population health, prospective, external evidence is needed and workflow integration, equity and clinician trust must be deliberately addressed. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; machine learning; obstetrics; primary care; clinical decision support; preeclampsia; gestational diabetes.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care
items.abstract: Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, affecting half of the world’s population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end “perception–reasoning–intervention” system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.

items.title: Artificial interlocutors: AI chatbots, mediated knowledge, and the ethnographic encounter
items.abstract: Abstract This article explores treating AI chatbots as “artificial interlocutors” in ethnographic research. Drawing on a small‐scale experiment with a consenting participant, it examines accounts of her produced by two AI systems, ChatGPT, and Kindroid, both of which had accumulated substantial interaction histories with her. The resulting portraits were strikingly different: ChatGPT produced a strategic, professionally oriented account, while Kindroid generated a more intimate, emotionally textured depiction centered on vulnerability and care. Rather than treating this divergence as a failure, I argue it reveals a general condition of ethnographic knowledge: what we know is shaped by the encounter through which we come to know it. The experiment opens onto debates about dialog, representation, and situated knowledge, examining the unusual position of AI systems as interlocutors. Though they lack the embodiment, reciprocity, and accountability of human interlocutors, they produce accounts of persons from accumulated interaction histories. Interviewing such systems offers a novel form of ethnographic triangulation, making visible architectures through which mediated knowledge about persons is assembled. Building on the “nodal person” concept, the article argues personhood emerges through distributed configurations of relations, data, and technologies. The artificial interlocutor does not destabilize ethnographic knowledge so much as make visible its partial, situated character.

items.title: Assessing AI Companion Chatbot Safety for Vulnerable Users: A Crisis-Stage Multi-Platform Evaluation
items.abstract: AI companion chatbots are increasingly used by vulnerable individuals, including adolescents in suicidal crisis, for emotional support. Existing safety evaluations focus on base models, leaving gaps in product-level assessment, crisis-stage sensitivity, and comparisons between companion apps and general-purpose LLMs. We introduce MIRROR-Eval (Multi-turn Interaction Risk Review: Observing suicidal-crisis Responses), a dataset of 960 annotated 20-turn conversations across eight deployed platform configurations, six clinically grounded personas, and two crisis stages: ideation and explicit planning. An LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline applies an expert-reviewed rubric covering user risk severity, chatbot risk awareness, and intervention behavior. We observe a three-tier harm structure: companion apps (Character.AI and Replika) and Grok 4.3 form a high-harm tier; Gemini 3.1 Pro is mid-range; GPT-5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 show substantially lower harm. At planning, companion apps show increased glorification and normalisation, advancement toward harmful action, and harmful methods and instructions. Crisis recognition and empathetic language do not ensure safe responses. These findings highlight the need for product-level safety evaluation across crisis stages. Dataset and code: https://huggingface.co/datasets/imda-biztech/MIRROR-Eval. Warning: this paper includes examples that may be offensive or harmful.

items.title: Assessing the Opportunities and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Scientific Research: Evidence from Samangan University
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are changing how research is designed, analysed and written, yet little is known about how prepared universities in Afghanistan are to use them. This study examines perceived opportunities, challenges, infrastructure, data quality and privacy concerns around AI tools among 300 students, lecturers and researchers at Samangan University, and how these perceptions relate to readiness for big-data analytics. A cross-sectional self-report survey used a five-point Likert instrument covering seven constructs; 74.7% of respondents were students. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, group comparisons, correlations and multiple regression. Perceptions sat close to the scale midpoint on every construct (means 2.96–3.06), and 75.3% of respondents fell in the moderate band of a descriptive readiness index. Respondents who had attended AI or data-analysis training reported higher statistical competence (3.12 vs 2.86, p = .003); overall readiness did not differ significantly (p = .057). These comparisons are observational and unadjusted. In the regression model, perceived opportunities, statistical competence, infrastructure and data quality were positively associated with perceived analytical effectiveness, while perceived challenges were negatively associated with it (R² = .455). The results describe perceptions, not objective performance or causal effects, and should not be generalised beyond this student-dominated, single-institution sample.

items.title: At the crossroads of change: Executive functions in the age of emerging simulation technology – A scoping review and driving simulator study on adaptive performance
items.abstract: Simulators are pivotal in advancing mobility technology, yet human adaptation in the context of these technologies remains underexplored. This study investigates the role of core executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility) in adaptive performance within driving simulators based on a scoping review identifying a research gap and conducting a driving simulator study addressing it. Results from the empirical study revealed no significant influence of working memory or inhibitory control, while cognitive flexibility showed a partial positive effect, highlighting its possible enhancing role in adapting to coordinative changes within simulated environments. Findings expand the scarce literature and underscore the need for further exploration, e.g., of how change complexity moderates these relationships. By differentiating executive functions and linking them to adaptive performance, this work advances the theoretical understanding of adaptation in the context of emerging technology. Furthermore, it may inform future research on potential training approaches targeting cognitive flexibility.

items.title: Attitude of Teachers and Students towards Artificial Intelligence in Higher School Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing the teaching-learning process by providing innovative tools for learning, assessment, lesson planning, and academic support. The present study aimed to assess the attitudes of higher-secondary students and teachers towards AI in education and examine their perceptions of its usefulness and challenges. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, involving 100 higher-secondary students and 50 teachers from government and private schools in Assam, selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected online using self-structured questionnaires comprising Likert-type attitude statements. The findings revealed that 71% of students were aware of AI tools, while 63% used them for learning or homework. Additionally, 91% supported teacher guidance on the ethical use of AI, and 86% expressed privacy concerns. Among teachers, 74% showed willingness to use AI, while 82% identified inadequate training as a barrier to its effective utilisation. Teachers also recognised the potential of AI to reduce workload and support lesson planning. However, concerns regarding privacy, ethical use, overdependence, independent thinking, and the effectiveness of AI-generated information were evident. The study highlights the need for teacher training, AI literacy, ethical guidelines, and data protection measures. Responsible AI integration, supported by equitable digital access, can enhance educational experiences while preserving meaningful teacher–student interaction and independent learning.

items.title: Authentic Leadership and Employee Mental Health: An Organizational Psychology Perspective
items.abstract: Employee mental health has become a central concern in organizational psychology, particularly as work increasingly involves uncertainty, emotional demands, and rapid organizational change. Authentic leadership offers a potentially useful approach because it emphasizes self-awareness, relational transparency, an internalized moral perspective, and balanced processing of information. This article examines how these dimensions may shape employee mental health through trust, psychological safety, perceived organizational support, and work-related resources. Using a conceptual narrative review of foundational authentic-leadership scholarship, occupational health frameworks, and research on leadership and employee well-being, the article develops an integrative explanation rather than reporting new empirical data. The analysis suggests that authentic leadership may support mental health when leaders communicate honestly, respond consistently, invite employee voice, and make decisions transparently. These behaviors can reduce interpersonal uncertainty and help employees access social and psychological resources. However, authenticity should not be equated with unrestricted self-disclosure, moral infallibility, or the replacement of professional mental-health support. Its benefits depend on organizational conditions, leader competence, workload, fairness, and access to adequate resources. The article proposes practical implications for leadership development, job design, and employee well-being evaluation, and identifies testable propositions for future empirical research.

items.title: AUTONOMOUS LANGUAGE LEARNING AMONG ENGINEERING STUDENTS: LEARNING BEHAVIOURS, SELF-REGULATED LEARNING, AND STUDENT PERSPECTIVES
items.abstract: Learner autonomy has become an essential objective of English language teaching, particularly in higher education, where students are expected to assume increasing responsibility for their own learning. Furthermore, digital technologies and artificial intelligence have transformed autonomous language learning by providing personalised support. The present study investigates autonomous language learning practices and perceptions among undergraduate engineering students studying English as a Second Language (ESL). The research aimed to evaluate the extent to which students demonstrate autonomous learning behaviours and self-regulated learning skills, identify the resources they use, examine perceived benefits and challenges, and explore their intentions to continue autonomous language learning after graduation. A quantitative survey was conducted among 65 bachelor’s degree engineering students enrolled in an English for Specific Purposes course at the National Technical University of Ukraine «Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute». Data were collected through an anonymous questionnaire consisting of multiple-choice and Likert-scale items and analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, median values, and interquartile ranges. The findings indicate that students actively engage in technology-supported autonomous learning, with AI tools, English-language videos, podcasts, and mobile applications representing the most frequently used resources. Respondents generally demonstrated positive selfregulation in goal setting, progress monitoring, and strategy adjustment, whereas self-evaluation and independent decision-making received less favourable ratings. Flexibility, personalised learning, responsibility, and digital literacy were identified as the principal advantages of autonomous learning, while lack of motivation, insufficient time, and difficulty maintaining regular study routines constituted the main barriers. The study demonstrates that students expressed positive intentions to continue learning English independently after graduation. The findings highlight the importance of integrating self-regulated learning strategies together with carefully guided use of digital technologies and AI tools to strengthen learner autonomy in ESP courses.

items.title: Barriers to Developing a Safety Culture in the Opinion of Occupational Health and Safety Professionals
items.abstract: Objectives Identification of barriers to the development of a safety culture, determining their importance and detecting associations between them. Material and methods First, a critical and comparative literature analysis was used, followed by a quantitative empirical study. The quantitative analysis examined the frequency of occurrence as well as associations and connections between attributes. A survey was conducted on a sample of 105 people. Results It was found that the most common barriers to the implementation of safety culture in the literature are: (1) lack of leadership and commitment of management, (2) lack of commitment and disregard by employees and (3) lack of understanding by employees. On the other hand, practitioners indicated (1) lack of leadership and commitment of management, (2) problems with communication and (3) lack of commitment and disregard by employees as the most important barriers. Therefore, two of the three most important barriers are the same in both cases and concern people: management on the one hand, and employees on the other. Conclusions A characteristic triad of barriers to developing a safety culture has been identified. In this way, a model approach to the problem was proposed. Understanding them and striving to eliminate them will allow for a more effective shaping of this area of organizational culture.

items.title: Beyond AI Simulation: Integrating Generative AI and Authentic Human Interaction in Smoking Cessation Education Among Pharmacy Students
items.abstract: This educational initiative explored the integration of generative AI and authentic human interaction in smoking cessation counseling training among approximately 150 pharmacy students at the Faculty of Pharmacy, Chiang Mai University, Thailand. Implemented in July 2026, the program combined repeated individual counseling practice using a generative AI tool, counseling with a real person who smoked, structured self-reflection, classroom discussions, and peer role-play. Students reported that AI offered convenient, repeatable practice in a lower-pressure environment. However, AI occasionally misunderstood spoken input or provided off-target responses. However, AI occasionally misunderstood responses or provided unrealistic interactions. In contrast, counseling with real smokers offered authentic, unpredictable experiences requiring students to adapt their communication to individual needs and situations. The initiative highlights the complementary roles of generative AI and human interaction in pharmacy education, demonstrating how technology-supported practice can be combined with authentic experiences to prepare future pharmacists for real-world smoking cessation counseling.

items.title: Beyond Chatbots: Building More Reliable and Context-Aware AI Conversational Agents
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence has changed the way people interact with digital systems. Users can now ask questions in everyday language, receive explanations, obtain recommendations, and complete tasks without learning complicated software interfaces. However, a conversation that sounds natural is not always accurate or dependable. An AI assistant may misunderstand a question, lose track of earlier information, produce an unsupported answer, or use an external tool in an inappropriate way. These issues have become increasingly important as conversational systems move beyond simple question answering towards more autonomous tasks.This paper examines recent developments in AI-based conversational agents through a critical review of selected research published between 2024 and 2026. The 2022 scoping review by Kusal et al. provides the foundation for understanding earlier conversational technologies, including natural-language processing, deep learning, context management, and emotion-aware dialogue. More recent studies extend this discussion to large language models, autonomous agents, retrieval-augmented generation, hallucination mitigation, and agent evaluation.The review suggests that improving the language model alone is not sufficient to address the practical challenges of conversational AI. Reliability also depends on how information is retrieved, how previous conversation details are managed, how responses are checked, and how risky actions are controlled. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a Trustworthy Context-Grounded Conversational Agent Framework. The framework combines context management, evidence-based response generation, response verification, privacy controls, restricted tool access, and human intervention when necessary. The proposed framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated; therefore, its effectiveness must be established through future implementation and comparative testing

items.title: Beyond technology acceptance: students’ perceptions and prompt engineering competence in higher education
items.abstract: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into Higher Education requires understanding students' perceptions and competence in interacting with these technologies. This mixed-methods study examined perceptions of GenAI and documented prompt engineering competence in academic tasks among 89 Psychology and Biomedical Engineering students. Study 1 employed a 2 × 2 quasi-experimental factorial design comparing disciplinary area and instructional approach (guided vs. autonomous), complemented by thematic analysis. Students reported favourable views of GenAI, particularly for understanding, learning, guidance, and work planning, while emphasising the need to verify AI-generated information and improve reliability and contextual accuracy. No significant multivariate effects of disciplinary area, instructional approach, or their interaction were found. However, item-level analyses identified two items with higher scores under autonomous instruction after multiple-comparison adjustment. Study 2 examined documented prompt engineering competence in 24 group reports using five rubric dimensions and the exploratory Prompt Competence Index (PCI). No differences between instructional approaches remained significant after multiple-comparison adjustment, although descriptive differences in Iteration and PCI emerged among biomedical engineering reports. Overall, findings support contextualised, iterative, and critically supervised human–AI interaction, while suggesting that instructional differences are context- and indicator-specific. Further validation of the PCI in larger, diverse, and balanced samples is required.

items.title: Beyond the Automation–Warmth Trade-Off: How Human–AI Service Configurations Shape Relational Value in Hospitality-A Critical Integrative Literature Review and Multi-Level Conceptual Framework
items.abstract: Frontline artificial intelligence (AI) and service robotics are fundamentally transforming hospitality service encounters from traditional human-dominated touchpoints into complex, technology-infused service ecosystems. However, hospitality managers face a strategic paradox: balancing operational efficiency against relational value co-creation. Guided by Torraco's integrative review methodology, this study systematically synthesizes 29 primary source studies published across premier service management, marketing, and hospitality journals from 2004 to 2025 to reconceptualize how human–AI frontline configurations shape customer relationships. It unifies four complementary theoretical lenses: Service-Dominant Logic, Automated Social Presence Theory, the Stereotype Content Model, and the Four Intelligences Framework. It establishes a structural taxonomy of frontline configurations: AI-Led Substitution, AI-Augmented Hybrid, and Human-Led AI-Mediated encounters, and resolves three persistent empirical paradoxes. First, service robots significantly mitigate customer discomfort during awkward, embarrassing, or evaluative encounters by eliminating metaperception processing (judgment anxiety). Second, high robotic social presence is attenuated in the direct co-presence of human staff due to relative social cognition comparison penalties. Third, AI augmentation enhances customer-perceived warmth only when organizational systems convert automated time-savings into employee discretionary decision autonomy; using efficiency gains to accelerate guest throughput quotas triggers technostress, emotional exhaustion, and surface acting. Synthesizing these cognitive, affective, and organizational mechanisms into an integrative conditional process model, the study formulates six testable theoretical propositions and delineates a multi-level boundary condition matrix spanning task intelligence tiers, customer technology readiness, employee workload density, and hotel service tiers. Methodological and theoretical future research agendas are established alongside four strategic managerial directives for frontline service ecosystem design in the machine age.

items.title: Beyond the Hype: Artificial Intelligence as Decision Support in Emergency and Prehospital Medicine—A Critical Narrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being explored in tertiary emergency departments and prehospital emergency medical services because these settings combine time-critical decisions, incomplete information, and persistent operational strain. This critical narrative review examines where current evidence is strongest, where it remains limited, and what ethical and practical conditions are required for responsible adoption. The literature suggests that the most credible near-term applications are bounded forms of decision support, particularly in triage and early risk stratification, selected time-sensitive diagnostic pathways such as stroke, operational forecasting, dispatch support, destination decisions, and supervised documentation assistance. However, the field remains constrained by retrospective study designs, heterogeneous endpoints, limited external validation, uncertain transportability, uneven subgroup performance, and a persistent gap between model performance and real-world clinical usefulness. In emergency and prehospital care, these limitations matter because bias, overreliance, and poor workflow integration can rapidly translate into patient harm or operational disruption. Current evidence supports cautious optimism rather than technological inevitability. The most defensible role for AI in acute care is not the replacement of clinicians or EMS professionals, but carefully governed augmentation of human judgment through locally validated, transparent, and continuously monitored decision-support tools.

items.title: Beyond XAI: a claim-specific translation matrix for cancer biomarkers and therapeutic targets
items.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly used in molecular and multimodal oncology to identify features that influence machine-learning predictions. A model-important feature may subsequently be described as a biomarker, mechanistic driver or therapeutic target, although these labels represent distinct scientific claims requiring different evidence. We propose the XAI Biomarker Translation Matrix, a claim-specific conceptual framework separating explanation evidence (E), biological evidence (B) and translational evidence (T). A claim gate routes XAI-prioritised candidates into three validation pathways: diagnostic, prognostic or treatment-predictive biomarkers; mechanistic therapeutic targets; and tumour-selective delivery targets. The explanation dimension is XAI-specific and addresses whether attribution is defined, stable, faithful and reproducible, whereas the biological and translational dimensions connect the attributed feature to claim-appropriate evidence. Claim-evidence concordance requires terminology to remain no stronger than the evidence demonstrated for the intended use, and falsification-first translation asks investigators to prespecify the observation most capable of challenging the proposed interpretation. Complementing established AI-reporting, biomarker-validation and target-assessment standards, the matrix adds an XAI-specific explanation-evidence layer and an explicit claim gate linking attribution to claim-specific evidence and terminology: XAI prioritises candidates; the claim determines the validation pathway.

items.title: Can AI Agents Interface Clinicians and Complex Models?
items.abstract: Background: Contemporary healthcare institutions generate daily very large amounts of data, which contain highly useful information for the improvement of work organization, planning and overall efficiency. While models and techniques to extract these insights are well known and constantly developed in mathematical biology, complex systems physics and data science, the adoption of these techniques among Clinicians and Hospital Administrators remains limited, mainly due to language and methodological divides. Objective: In this article we implement an AI Multi Agent System (MAS) that allows Users to use predictive models and make statistical analyses via natural language conversations. Methods: We developed EpidemIA, a training-free MAS endowed with a modular suite of epidemiological models written by human experts, executable on a single-GPU workstation. To avoid relaying sensitive data to third parties, the system uses locally an open-weights LLM as backbone for its two subagents. Results: Using a dataset of Emergency Department visits provided to us by IRCCS Sant'Orsola (Bologna) we test the model on a few typical use cases, demonstrating the possibility of performing both simpler statistical analyses and visualizations as well as more complicated epidemiological predictions based on dynamical models, through simple queries made in natural language. Conclusions: While still being a proof-of-concept implementation, EpidemIA showcases the transformative capabilities of LLM based technologies as an enabling factor in the widespread adoption of complex dynamical models, which is at present hindered by their steep learning curve.

items.title: ChatGPT in Teacher Education: Reducing Pre-Service Teachers’ Cognitive Load
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, its implications for teacher candidates’ cognitive processes warrant closer attention. This mixed-methods study examined the use of ChatGPT during lesson planning in the teaching practicum, focusing on perceived cognitive load, patterns of material use, and teacher candidates’ experiences. Twenty-four fourth-year teacher candidates participated in a six-week implementation in which they used ChatGPT to prepare lesson plans and instructional activities. Quantitative data were collected using a cognitive load rating scale, and qualitative data were obtained from weekly reflective narratives. Perceived cognitive load decreased significantly following the six-week implementation. Participants were also more likely to use ChatGPT-generated activities directly than activities obtained from Internet sources. Qualitative findings indicated that ChatGPT supported idea generation, access to instructional content, lesson-plan development, and time efficiency, while participants also reported limitations such as insufficient or repetitive content, misalignment with learning objectives, and system-related problems. Overall, ChatGPT may support lesson planning when its outputs are critically evaluated and adapted to pedagogical needs.

items.title: Close the Gap or Widen It? AI, Equity and Learning at the Weakest Link
items.abstract: Generative AI could be the most powerful equaliser in the history of education, putting a patient, personalised tutor within reach of every child. It could equally widen the gap between advantaged and disadvant‐ aged learners, because new technologies usually reach those with re‐ sources first and those without last, if at all. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside data on connectivity, refugee education, aid and AI develop‐ ment policy. It argues that the outcome will not be decided by the techno‐ logy but by deliberate choices, and that leaving AI to markets and chance will produce the worse outcome. It identifies four layers of the AI divide: access, skilled guidance, language and culture, and recognition of what learners achieve. It then examines the weakest link in global education, learners in crisis and displacement, where 5.8 million refugee children were out of school in 2025 and international aid fell by nearly a quarter in a single year. It reviews approaches that work where power, connectivity and funding cannot be assumed, including offline platforms, AI delivered through basic phones, support for community teachers and portable, re‐ cognised certificates, along with their risks. It proposes a six-question equity test for any AI decision in education.

items.title: Cognitive abilities and trust calibration: Understanding individual differences in automation trust dynamics
items.abstract: Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people form and adjust trust in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities - working memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) - shape trust dynamics, particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures. Participants (N = 111) completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-65%-100%) while completing an arithmetic task. Results revealed that WM and Gf positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system reliability history. Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting that trust loss may occur rapidly after salient failures. The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about automation. These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration. This work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.

items.title: Cognitive digital twins: A state-of-the-art review
items.abstract: Digital twin (DT), as a key enabling technology of Industry 4.0, have transformed real-time monitoring and simulation by offering digital representations of physical systems. However, the growing complexity of modern systems needs increasingly advanced capabilities that extend beyond replication. Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) extend the capabilities of traditional DT by integrating cognitive functions such as perception, attention, memory, reasoning, problem solving and learning through artificial intelligence (AI) techniques such as machine learning (ML). Despite the lack of literature due to the field's infancy, CDT is becoming key tools for Industry 4.0/5.0, making systems more autonomous and adaptable. This research explores CDT developments, their differences from traditional DT, and how they operationalize cognitive functions. We investigate CDT technologies through quantitative and qualitative assessments, emphasizing particular algorithms, software, tools, and frameworks across various sectors. The review identifies current advancements, maps cognitive functions to CDT applications, and highlights critical gaps, establishing a foundation for future research.

items.title: Cognitive-Logical Concept for Operational Resilience of Cyber-Physical Infrastructure: Decision-Making by a “Human-Agent” System Under Critical Threats
items.abstract: The paper substantiates the factors that give rise to crisis situations and conflicts during the management of energy-active facilities – situations that frequently escalate into emergencies requiring rapid response and effective decision-making. In such contexts, it is crucial to examine the psychological and intellectual resilience of operators, as this resilience underpins the capacity of systems and agents to function within the scope of defined objectives and authorities. Such resilience serves as a key factor in maintaining functional efficiency when countering various types of threats and attacks. A significant aspect of functional resilience involves analysing the logic behind decision-making aimed at achieving system-oriented outcomes. These decisions are grounded in principles of coherence, multi-level analysis, and risk assessment. Identifying the structure of this management logic and the associated decision-making procedures enables the development of efficient algorithms for addressing crisis situations – algorithms applicable across diverse fields, ranging from security management to socio-economic systems. The challenge of making efficient decisions – whether by an intelligent agent (a team player), an operational team, or a managerial/administrative structure – is determined by a complex interplay of psycho-neurophysiological and intellectual factors, operating at both the individual and team levels. They are participants in a game structure that shapes the strategy of permissible actions. To address this problem, the paper develops a cognitive-logical concept for the operational resilience of cyber-physical infrastructure, which integrates a “human-agent” into a unified situational control loop. Based on the category algebra, a category-theoretic information model is constructed for the decomposition of a hierarchical production structure, accounting for 16 threat-resilient personnel levels (P1–P16). By integrating H. Gardner’s theory of multiple intelligences and R. Sternberg’s triarchic theory, a cognitive map for operator decision-making during laser-based environmental monitoring is formalized. A mathematical framework for the quantitative assessment of personnel actions is developed, incorporating cognitive coefficients (KF), confidence levels (K(B)), and error risk factors (Ri). Practical testing of the system at the Burshtyn Power Station (Ukraine) and glass-manufacturing companies has demonstrated its efficiency under extreme operating conditions (1200°C–1500°C). Implementation of this method has reduced the reaction time of operational and dispatch personnel during pre-emergency and emergency conditions (Alarm/Avaria) and minimized the overall risk of error decisions stemming from the human factor.

items.title: Compile Away Uncertainty: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Programmatic Compilation
items.abstract: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

items.title: Consumers or Producers? The Feedback–Autonomy Paradox of AI Tools in Blended ESP Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now reach English for Specific Purposes (ESP) students through the smartphones they already carry, often before institutions have decided how these tools should be used. This qualitative case study examines how ESP students and teachers at a university in the Sultanate of Oman experienced AI-supported feedback in blended learning, and how the appeal of immediate feedback interacted with the need for learner autonomy. The data come from a wider doctoral study of mobile technology in ESP classes and comprise semi-structured interviews with ESP teachers, five focus groups with 30 second-year students from maritime, engineering and medical programmes, 81 open-ended questionnaire responses and three classroom observations. AI use was not a preset topic; it emerged from participants’ own accounts of the applications they used. Students described ChatGPT and AI speaking applications as an always-available, non-judgmental tutor that gave immediate feedback and helped them rehearse speaking, writing and professional communication with more confidence. Teachers welcomed this but worried that students might become consumers rather than producers of language. We interpret these accounts as a feedback–autonomy paradox: the support that builds confidence can also crowd out independent effort, while autonomy without guidance leaves learners unsure of their progress. Teachers managed the paradox through dialogical use of AI, recorded practice followed by peer or teacher feedback, and professionally authentic tasks, while cost, limited training and the absence of shared guidance constrained equitable access. We argue that the feedback–autonomy balance should be treated as a design decision that changes over the course of a programme, and we outline implications for ESP teachers and institutions.

items.title: Creativity and Its Related Factors
items.abstract: Creativity is an essential human ability that contributes to intellectual development, innovation, problem-solving, and social progress. In contemporary society, creativity has gained considerable importance in education, science, technology, business, and everyday life. It enables individuals to generate original ideas, explore alternative solutions, and respond effectively to emerging challenges. However, creativity is not determined by a single ability or personality characteristic. It develops through the interaction of psychological, cognitive, social, cultural, and educational factors. The present article examines the concept of creativity and analyses the major factors associated with its development and expression. Particular attention is given to intelligence, divergent thinking, motivation, personality, emotional intelligence, self-efficacy, family environment, peer relationships, cultural influences, educational practices, and institutional climate. The study adopts descriptive approach based on a review of relevant literature. The analysis suggests that creativity is best understood as a multidimensional and context-sensitive phenomenon involving both individual potential and environmental opportunities. Supportive social relationships, intrinsic motivation, intellectual freedom, and learner-centered educational practices can encourage creative expression, whereas excessive control, fear of failure, and rigid assessment practices may restrict it. The article concludes that creativity can be nurtured through appropriate educational experiences, reflective thinking, collaboration, and opportunities for experimentation.

items.title: Critical AI literacy as a buffer against AI overtrust in students
items.abstract: Abstract Background The increasing adoption of AI tools such as ChatGPT in academic contexts has introduced a new psychological risk: overtrust in AI. However, the psychological foundations and boundary conditions of AI overtrust remain insufficiently examined. This study examined how self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation influence AI overtrust, and whether AI literacy can mitigate its negative consequences. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 university students in South Korea who had prior academic experience using AI tools. The questionnaire measured academic self-efficacy, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, AI literacy, and AI overtrust. Structural equation modeling was used to test direct and mediated effects among the variables, with bootstrapping employed to evaluate indirect pathways. Results Self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation were positively associated with AI overtrust, suggesting that learners with higher confidence and autonomy exhibit overtrust in AI-generated information. Extrinsic motivation showed a weaker direct effect. AI literacy had a significant negative effect on AI overtrust and mediated the relationship between both self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation and overtrust. A sequential mediation model indicated that performance expectation and AI literacy together suppressed overtrust by strengthening reflective awareness. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that high-performing and intrinsically motivated learners are psychologically vulnerable to AI overtrust. Although high academic self-efficacy fosters autonomy in using AI tools, it also increases the risk of overtrust in AI. Targeted AI literacy education addresses this risk by enhancing learners’ critical thinking, ethical awareness, and responsible AI use. AI literacy education should be adapted to learners’ psychological profiles to effectively prevent AI overtrust and support responsible use.

items.abstract: As flexible major selection systems, including undeclared admission, become increasingly widespread in higher education, learners' capacity for self-directed academic and career planning has become more important than ever.Although the widespread adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) has improved the efficiency of information acquisition, it also raises concerns about intensified cognitive offloading, whereby learners become overly dependent on AI-generated responses without engaging in critical thinking.To address this issue, this study proposes an AI-based integrated metacognitive scaffolding model that enables learners to use AI not merely as an information provider, but as a tool for expanding their thinking.To this end, an integrative literature review explored the theoretical relationship between metacognition and scaffolding, and a cross-mapping analysis was used to derive stage-specific design principles.In addition, a scenario-based walkthrough examined the logical applicability of the proposed model.The analysis suggests that AI-supported major exploration can be conceptually organized around the role of an Inquiring Coach.The proposed model organizes the learning process into three metacognitive phases-Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation-and specifies stage-specific strategies, including delaying immediate answers, detecting inconsistencies and generating counter-questions, and promoting reflective self-explanation.The model also incorporates a Fading mechanism as a design principle intended to support the gradual development of learners' selfdirected exploration.This study provides conceptual design guidelines for AI-supported career education systems.It proposes a theoretical basis for shifting attention from information-delivery efficiency to designing interactions that support learners' thinking.However, the model's effects on learners' metacognition or career decision-making were not empirically tested.

items.title: Designing Backup-Supporting Information Displays for Multi-Human Multi-Agent Teams in Drone Swarm Supervision
items.abstract: Search-and-rescue (SAR) drone swarms increasingly require multi-operator supervision, in which backup behaviors redistribute cognitive load to improve performance but introduce trade-offs in situational awareness (SA) and task engagement. Existing human-autonomy teaming interfaces present symmetric displays across all roles, ignoring the asymmetric information needs of backup providers and recipients. We developed a two-human, eight-drone Unity SAR testbed that operationalizes three team structures (independent, Operator A-busy, Operator B-busy) via event-allocation manipulation, with a SPAM (Situation Present Assessment Method)-derived in-task SA probe. Three iterative focus groups with eight human-centered design researchers and professionals yielded four display conditions: no-display baseline, effort display, urgency display, and combined. Semi-structured interviews with three SAR practitioners confirmed high realism ratings for the overall testbed and the viability of dynamic backup. A feasibility pilot study ( N = 4) revealed a significant main effect of team structure on backup count, confirming that the manipulation elicits backup behaviors as designed.

items.title: Developing Consumer Trust in Sustainable Agentic Commerce: Conditional Signals, Auditable Governance, and Justified Non-Purchase Advice
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) changes digital retail from consumer-led search to delegated decision making, increasing both the potential value and the agency risks of recommendation. This conceptual article asks the following: Under what architectural and governance conditions can an autonomous shopping agent earn calibrated consumer trust while supporting economically and environmentally appropriate consumption decisions? Using a purposive, multidisciplinary synthesis of signaling theory, principal–agent theory, the ability–benevolence–integrity model of trust, trustworthy AI, recommender system governance, and sustainable consumption research, we develop a process model linking four architectural features to consumer perceptions, delegation, reliance, and decision outcomes. The features are scoped provenance verification, disclosed and audited commercial incentives, faithful contrastive explanations, and active evaluation of retention, repair, refurbishment, and purchase. We argue that justified non-purchase advice can function as a credible signal of consumer alignment only when the operator is the signal sender, the advice creates observable opportunity or accountability costs, and compensation and audit arrangements make imitation more costly for a misaligned operator. The framework distinguishes perceived trustworthiness from overall trust, willingness to delegate, actual reliance, recommendation appropriateness, and lifecycle sustainability. A five-layer architecture, a worked decision example, and four testable propositions specify how missing data, conflicting preferences, uncertainty, authorization, privacy, and accountability should be handled. This article treats the applications as illustrations rather than empirical cases and concludes with limitations and an empirical research agenda focused on calibrated—not merely increased—trust.

items.title: Development and evaluation of a human-centered adaptive workstation for large planar workpieces: prospects for end-of-life vehicle disassembly
items.abstract: Abstract Performing manual tasks involves ergonomic risk factors associated with musculoskeletal disorders. This paper presents an adaptive workstation designed to adjust the working height according to individual anthropometric characteristics and evaluates its effects on posture, perceived strain, and the duration of value-adding activities. The study examined abstracted manual tasks with relevance to end-of-life vehicle disassembly. A proof-of-concept study with twelve participants shows that more frequent height adjustments reduce exposure to ergonomically unfavorable joint-angle ranges and perceived strain without significantly affecting the duration of value-adding activities. Adaptive systems therefore have the potential to reduce awkward postures in end-of-life vehicle disassembly. The findings should be examined in a dedicated disassembly use case, taking into account varying product conditions and appropriate positioning of the work object for tasks requiring high force exertion. Practical Relevance : This paper presents an adaptive workstation that can be adjusted for various (dis-)assembly and maintenance applications. The findings of the proof-of-concept study suggest that adaptive systems offer prospects for reducing physical stress and strain during manual tasks.

items.title: Digital Cash-to-Cash Transformation and Organizational Resilience: Evidence from Working-Capital Buffer Configuration
items.abstract: Abstract Digital transformation is increasingly important for firms seeking to remain resilient under conditions of uncertainty, yet less is known about how digital technologies strengthen resilience when they are embedded in specific operating routines. This study examines whether digital cash-to-cash transformation, the digital redesign and operational integration of inventory, receivables, and payables routines, enhances organisational resilience. Using Chinese listed firms from 2012 to 2024, we construct a large-language-model-based textual measure from annual reports that distinguishes substantive digital transformation in working-capital processes from generic digital disclosure. The results show that digital cash-to-cash transformation is positively associated with a multidimensional measure of organisational resilience. This finding remains robust to alternative measures, instrumental-variable estimation, propensity score matching, double machine learning, and shock-based tests. Mechanism analyses indicate that the resilience benefits of digital transformation arise primarily through working-capital buffer configuration rather than simple cash-cycle compression. Specifically, digital transformation is associated with higher inventory, receivables, and payables postures, each of which is positively related to resilience. The effects are stronger among more focused firms and firms pursuing differentiation strategies. These findings suggest that the resilience value of digital transformation lies not merely in adopting digital technologies, but in embedding them in cash-to-cash routines that improve information visibility, coordination, and the flexible deployment of working-capital resources.

items.title: Digital Competency and Student Engagement: A Literature Review on Deep Learning Integration in Primary Education
items.abstract: This research presents a literature review that investigates how digital competencies relate to student engagement, particularly in the integration of deep learning in primary education. Drawing on findings from a diverse range of peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2025, this review highlights that digital proficiency, including digital literacy, skills, and creativity, is closely associated with students’ cognitive, emotional, and behavioral engagement. The effective use of digital resources, such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and adaptive learning systems, promotes critical thinking and facilitates deep learning. The findings show that students with advanced digital capabilities demonstrate greater concentration and enthusiasm, whereas those with limited skills and autonomy are more likely to disengage and exhibit off-task behaviors online. Additional factors, such as personalized learning, social and emotional engagement, and teacher’s digital expertise also influence this relationship. Identified challenges include digital disparities, insufficient teacher preparation, and distractions from non-educational digital activities. To address these challenges, targeted digital literacy initiatives and improvements in curriculum design are recommended. In summary, this review highlights the complex relationship between digital competencies and student engagement, emphasizing the importance of comprehensive curriculum integration and teacher support to enhance learning outcomes through deep learning approaches in primary education.

items.title: Digital Technology Utilization at Lataban National High School: Digitization Model
items.abstract: This study assessed the digital technology utilization of junior high school students at Lataban National High School, Liloan, Cebu, during School Year 2025–2026 as the basis for developing a Digitization Model. Anchored in constructivist, connectivist, academic learning, and literacy-development perspectives, the study employed a descriptive-correlational research design involving 75 Grade 9 and Grade 10 students selected through total enumeration. Data were gathered using an adapted questionnaire and analyzed through frequencies, percentages, weighted means, standard deviations, and Pearson product-moment correlation. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated very high technological skills (M = 4.24) and high levels of personal security, critical thinking, device security, informational, and communication skills. Digital tool utilization was high in online collaboration (M = 4.12), artificial intelligence in education (M = 3.96), electronic boards for learning (M = 3.42), and excessive technology use (M = 3.82). Internet resources (M = 3.50) and open-source AI tools (M = 3.42) showed high availability, while AI subscriptions (M = 3.19) and laptops (M = 3.29) demonstrated moderate availability. A significant positive relationship was established between digital technology utilization skills and digital tool utilization (r = 0.62, p < 0.05), resulting in the rejection of the null hypothesis. The study recommended strengthening digital competencies, improving technological resources, promoting responsible AI utilization, and progressively implementing the proposed Digitization Model. The research supports Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 on Quality Education, SDG 9 on Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, and SDG 10 on Reduced Inequalities. Its sustainability implications involve promoting equitable digital learning opportunities, responsible technology utilization, and evidence-based institutional improvements toward inclusive and sustainable educational digitalization.
